text:
alex: Quick perf sweep across microbatch sizes for streaming chat vs non-streaming completions on the rtx-a100 cluster. TL;DR: streaming needs very small microbatches (1-2) to hit p99 SLOs; non-streaming can batch up to 8 for much higher throughput with acceptable p95. Dashboard: https://redwood.internal/perf/runs/1782457001

maya: Nice. Do you see kernel selection flipping between runs? Did you force any kernel flags?

alex: Kernel selection did flip. For streaming (mostly 1 token increments) the runtime picked the small-token optimized kernel (fast single-step attention). For bulk completions with longer seqs it preferred the fused attention kernel. I also tried forcing fused on streaming and it regressed first-token latency.

ryan: Can you paste the exact harness config so I can reproduce locally?

alex: ```json
{
  "model": "redwood/1.3b-opt",
  "microbatch_sizes": [1,2,4,8,16],
  "streaming": true,\n  "kernel_policy": "auto",\n  "kv_cache": "enabled",\n  "batch_timeout_ms": 50
}
```

liz: What were the p95/p99 numbers?

alex: From the synthetic harness (short prompts distribution):
- streaming, microbatch=1: p95=120ms, p99=280ms
- streaming, microbatch=2: p95=140ms, p99=460ms
- streaming, microbatch=4: p95=90ms, p99=900ms (tail explodes due to queuing)
- non-streaming, batch=8: p95=220ms, p99=450ms, throughput ~3x vs streaming baseline

maya: That matches intuition: waiting for microbatch fill reduces avg latency but creates long tails when one request waits for others.

ryan: Are these harness numbers or sampled from prod?

alex: Harness + a small sample from production traces. Prod shows the same pattern when traffic mixes streaming and non-streaming: large batches occasionally absorb a streaming request and push its p99 much higher.

liz: Any mitigation ideas? Adaptive sizing?

maya: We could implement a simple policy: if request.stream==true then cap microbatch to 2. Non-streaming requests can use larger targets or longer timeouts. Also consider preemptive service for the first token of streaming flows.

alex: I prototyped a policy: streaming_flag -> max_microbatch=2; additionally if GPU idle >200ms allow burst_merge. Also added kernel fallback: if end-to-end p99 > 500ms, fallback to the lower-variance kernel even if cost is higher. Results looked promising in lab.

sre-bot: incident-check: no alerts triggered during run 1782457001

ryan: Can you paste the perf profile (flame/stack breakdown) lines you captured?

alex: ```
[PROFILE] run=1782457001: queue_wait_mean=18ms queue_wait_p99=420ms
[PROFILE] kernel_exec_mean=60ms kernel_exec_p99=120ms
[PROFILE] kv_cache_hit_rate=86% (streaming)
[PROFILE] overhead_scheduler=8ms
```

maya: Interesting — the queue_wait_p99 is the big offender for microbatch>2. That suggests the tail is queuing-dominated rather than kernel exec.

liz: Another mitigation: two-path serving. Low-latency lane with tiny queues + single-step kernels for streaming. Bulk lane with larger accumulators for completions. Route by request.stream flag.

alex: Agreed. Also trying kv_prefetch for streaming so first token doesn't wait for backend cache warmup.

maya: Could also experiment with dynamic microbatch sizing: start with max=2, if a given window shows high idle GPU time then opportunistically increase batch target for a short period.

alex: I'll run an A/B next week: baseline vs adaptive cap + kernel fallback + kv_prefetch. I'll post run ids and graphs.
